concepts.title: Citizenship as Full and Equal Membership

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Citizenship as Full and Equal Membership' refers to.
questions.a: Citizenship names full and equal membership of a political community: citizens enjoy equal rights, owe the community their allegiance and take part in its collective decisions. It marks the difference between belonging to a country as a stakeholder and merely living on its territory as a foreigner.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Citizenship as Full and Equal Membership'.
questions.a: Citizen means insider with equal rights and shared fate; the outsider may reside but does not rule.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Citizenship as Full and Equal Membership' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Citizenship in India: Acquisition and Termination

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Citizenship in India: Acquisition and Termination' refers to.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution's citizenship part empowers Parliament to fix the rules. Indian law grants citizenship by birth, by descent, by registration, by naturalisation after residence, and by incorporating territory; it can be lost by renunciation, by acquiring another citizenship, or by deprivation for specified offences.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Citizenship in India: Acquisition and Termination'.
questions.a: Five doors in, three routes out -- citizenship status is legally made and legally unmade.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Citizenship in India: Acquisition and Termination' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Universal Citizenship and Its Critics: Gender and Class

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Universal Citizenship and Its Critics: Gender and Class' refers to.
questions.a: Formal citizenship promises identical rights for all, but critics note that identical rules can freeze real inequality. Feminists point out that the public-private split long kept women's work invisible in the political community; socialist critics show that poverty bars the poor from exercising citizenship that exists only on paper.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Universal Citizenship and Its Critics: Gender and Class'.
questions.a: Same legal box, different lives -- universal citizenship must still answer to gender and class realities.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Universal Citizenship and Its Critics: Gender and Class' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Minority Rights, Cultural Rights and Multicultural Citizenship

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Minority Rights, Cultural Rights and Multicultural Citizenship' refers to.
questions.a: In societies with many cultures, equal citizenship may require more than identical treatment: minorities may need special cultural rights -- language protection, educational autonomy, personal law -- to participate with dignity. Multicultural citizenship thus blends common civic status with group-differentiated rights, while guarding against practices that crush members' individual freedom.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Minority Rights, Cultural Rights and Multicultural Citizenship'.
questions.a: Equal citizenship in a diverse land may need unequal cultural provisions -- so long as members stay free inside their group.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Minority Rights, Cultural Rights and Multicultural Citizenship' taught, and from which source text?
